Last quarter my manager, Darshan, walked into our bay grinning. "Customers who use the new help chat spend thirty percent more. Put it in the board deck: chat drives sales."
I'm Parul, and I've learned to be the annoying one in these moments. I asked three questions out loud. Could a third thing cause both? People buying expensive fridges ask more questions and also spend more. Could it run backwards? Maybe spending more makes you need help, not the other way round. Could it be a fluke of one festive month?
Darshan sighed. "So what do you want?"
"A comparison group. Show the chat button to half the visitors at random for four weeks, and hide it from the other half."
We did. The gap shrank to three percent. Real, but small.
The board deck said three. Darshan grumbled, then thanked me in the meeting.

qa.q: How much more did chat users spend, according to Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan said customers who used the new help chat spent thirty percent more.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling when Darshan wanted to claim that chat drives sales?
qa.a: Parul felt cautious and a little uneasy, wary that a third cause, reversed direction or a festive fluke could explain the link.

qa.q: Why was the comparison group the right next step?
qa.a: Showing the chat to a random half of visitors separated the chat's real effect from big spenders asking more questions, and revealed only a small gap.

qa.q: How might Darshan feel when the gap shrank to three percent?
qa.a: Darshan was probably disappointed and a bit grumpy at losing the big claim, but grateful enough to thank Parul in the meeting.

grounding: Shows a careful analyst asking about third causes, reverse direction and coincidence, and using a comparison group before claiming cause.

Supervisor's note, public health data unit. Written by Mohit, team lead.
This week Yogesh, our newest analyst, was asked to confirm a link for a district report: villages with more mobile phone towers had more reported fever cases.
Several people in the office had already decided the towers were the cause. Yogesh didn't argue. He listed other possibilities on the whiteboard: bigger villages get more towers and also have more clinics that report fever; more towers could mean better roads, so more people reach a clinic; and the data came from one monsoon season.
Then he asked for a comparison: villages of the same size, with and without new towers, over three years. Once size was matched, the link almost vanished.
What I did next: I asked Yogesh to present his whiteboard to the whole unit on Friday, and added his three questions to our report checklist.

qa.q: What link was Yogesh asked to confirm?
qa.a: That villages with more mobile phone towers had more reported fever cases.

qa.q: Why did Yogesh stay calm when others had decided the towers were the cause?
qa.a: Yogesh felt curious rather than alarmed, and was careful to check whether village size, roads or one monsoon season explained the link.

qa.q: What made Yogesh's comparison fair?
qa.a: Matching villages of the same size, with and without new towers, over three years removed the size effect, and the link almost vanished.

qa.q: How did Mohit see Yogesh's work?
qa.a: Mohit was impressed enough to ask Yogesh to present on Friday and to add the three questions to the report checklist.

grounding: Shows a careful young analyst asking about third causes and one-season coincidence and finding a comparison group before claiming cause.

Tuesday.
Shalini ma'am announced today that front-row students score higher, so from Monday the weakest kids move to the front. Everyone clapped.
I didn't. I kept thinking. Who chooses the front row? The keen kids, the ones whose parents push them, the ones who can see the board. So maybe keenness causes both the seat and the marks. Or maybe it runs backwards: kids who do well feel confident sitting up front. Or maybe it's just this one batch.
After the meeting I asked her if we could try it properly: move seats by lottery in two sections for a term, keep the other two as they are, and compare. She laughed and said I sound like a scientist, but agreed to try it in Class 7.
It might still help. I just want to know it helps before we tell parents it does.
Bhupen

qa.a: Shalini ma'am announced that front-row students score higher, so the weakest kids will move to the front from Monday.

qa.a: Moving seats by lottery in two sections for a term and comparing them with two unchanged sections gives a comparison group before claiming cause.

qa.q: How does Shalini ma'am react to the idea?
qa.a: Shalini ma'am is amused and calls Bhupen a scientist, but is open enough to agree to a trial in Class 7.

This summer the heat was so bad that our school closed early. I'm Sahil. One evening I did a silly dance on the terrace, spinning with my arms out, and shouted, "Come, rain!" An hour later it poured. I was sure I had done it.
The next day I did the dance again. Nothing. I told my cousin Saurabh I must have spun the wrong way.
Saurabh laughed and showed me the weather report on his phone. It had said rain was coming that evening, two days before I ever danced.
I still dance when it's hot. But now I know the clouds were already on their way.

Class 4 teacher's note, January. Written by Lalit, class teacher.
Kunal came back today after three days of fever. He told the class, very seriously, "I had ice cream at my cousin's wedding on Saturday, and then I got fever. Ice cream in winter makes you sick." Two children vowed never to eat ice cream again.
Half the class had coughs that week, and the boy beside Kunal was sick on Friday, before the wedding.
What I did next: I didn't tell Kunal he was wrong. I asked the class for other reasons someone might get a fever in January. They listed germs, sick friends and cold air. Kunal said, "Maybe it was the cough going round." I reminded everyone to wash hands and to tell a grown-up if they feel unwell.

qa.q: Why did Kunal feel sure the ice cream caused the fever?

qa.q: Why was Lalit's question to the class a good approach?
qa.a: Asking for other reasons someone might get a fever let the children, and Kunal, think of the cough going round themselves instead of just being told they were wrong.

qa.q: How might the two children who vowed never to eat ice cream feel?
qa.a: They were probably worried and a bit scared, believing ice cream could make them sick too.

grounding: Shows a child who believes eating ice cream once caused his fever because the fever came afterwards, seen in a teacher's winter note.

Last winter my father had a bad cough that wouldn't go, and within a day the family group was full of cures. I'm Vidya, the only one in the house studying science, so everyone forwarded everything to me.
One message said a man drank a leaf-and-honey paste and "the next morning, cough gone!" Another was a video of a woman crying with joy after taking a herbal powder. The timing made them sound so convincing: took it, then recovered.
But I kept thinking: how many people took the paste and didn't get better? They don't make videos. And lots of coughs get better on their own. The paste just happened to be there when that happened.
Still, it was exhausting to be the one saying "wait". I felt like the family villain.
In the end Karthik, my cousin who's a nurse, backed me, and Papa went to the doctor that evening.

Kunal, second year, came in looking tired. His phone had forty unread forwards from his family group, most about his father's knee pain. One said an uncle's neighbour rubbed on a herbal oil and "walked normally the next day". Another promised a powder that "fixed joint pain in one week".

Anirban keeps sending me the same video. A guy with perfect hair says he drank warm lemon water every morning and his headaches "vanished in three days". Anirban means well. He's watched me hold my head through lectures all week.

Shreya's lower back had ached for two weeks, and the office move meant carrying boxes up three floors with a deadline on Friday.
Farhan slid a copper bracelet across her desk. "Magnetic. My back was killing me, I put this on, and in a week, gone."

Farhan blinked. "How would I know?"
"Exactly. Did anyone try it against a fake bracelet and compare?"
"You're overthinking a bracelet."
Maybe. But one person's before-and-after proved very little. A real test needed lots of people, some with the thing and some without, and nobody knowing which.
She handed the bracelet back with a smile, booked the company doctor's lunchtime slot for Thursday, and asked a colleague to help with the heavy boxes.

Jomon, you're sulking because your friends didn't want to play your game at Onam? Listen to your Seema Ammachi. Let me tell you about my brother Babu.
One Onam, when Babu was nine, he decided the sadya for his friends would be his. He loved bitter-gourd pachadi more than anything, so he told our Amma to make three times as much. "Everyone loves it," he said. He never asked.

Sahil,
You won't believe my week. You know that singer from the reality show, the one with the dyed hair? I think his songs are the most overrated thing on earth. So on Monday I posted in the class group: "Can we admit his new album is trash? Obviously everyone thinks so."
I thought I was saying what everyone was thinking. Everyone I talk to at the bus stop can't stand him.
Forty-two messages later, I found out half the class loves him. One girl said I insult everything I don't understand. Someone else called me a snob. It felt like the whole class had turned on me. I barely slept.

Kalyani, you asked what happened at Diwali dinner. Okay. I'm Sachin, and I made a fool of myself.
Everyone at my college thinks arranged marriage is outdated. My flatmates, my class, every reel I scroll past. So when Mausi asked about my plans, I said, "Nobody my age wants an arranged marriage any more. That's over."

I felt my face go hot. I'd said "nobody" like it was a fact. Turns out I'd just never asked anyone outside my flat.
I still know what I want for myself. But I've stopped saying "nobody" and "everybody". At the next dinner I'm going to ask more and announce less.

Sarika, you asked how I got better at my job this year. Honestly? I stopped trusting my own head. I'm Anjali, and I design sign-up forms for a bank.
Last spring I was sure everyone hated long forms. I hate them, my team hates them. So I built a one-page sign-up. Then I made myself do something uncomfortable: I sat in a branch in Lucknow for two days and asked customers, mostly older people and small shopkeepers, to try it.

Now, whenever I'm surprised by what someone thinks, I write it in a little notebook. Surprise means I was assuming. The notebook is nearly full.
